found: Based on mid-points of closing option bid and ask quotes, a portfolio strategy that each month buys (sells) initially delta-hedged at-the-money call options on stocks with low (high) volatility and holds for one month generates an average return of about 2% per month. The average return decreases systematically with the market capitalization of the underlying stock. ... Adding trading friction equal to 50%, 75% or 100% of the closing option bid-ask spread incrementally reduces average profitability from about 1% per month to approximately zero.
suggested_fix: Cao & Han (Journal of Financial Economics, 2013) find that delta-hedged equity option returns fall monotonically with the underlying stock's idiosyncratic volatility. According to a secondary summary of their 2010 working paper, a strategy that buys delta-hedged calls on low-volatility stocks and sells them on high-volatility stocks earns about 2% per month at mid quotes. Paying 50% of the bid-ask spread cuts that to about 1%, and paying 100% cuts it to roughly zero. The return also shrinks as the underlying's market capitalization rises.

suggested_fix: IVolatility reports (a self-published vendor study) on 9,622 S&P 500 earnings ATM straddles from 2021-2026. Each straddle used options with about 9 DTE, was bought at the ask at the close just before the print and was sold at the bid at the close just after it. The trades had a 22.0% win rate and a mean P&L of -18.47% per trade. The quintile where implied move most exceeded historical realized move lost 44.5% per trade, while the most underpriced quintile earned +36.7%.
